segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to the other side of the sea, to the region of the Gerasenes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he got out of the boat, immediately a man with an unclean spirit came out of the tombs to meet him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He had his dwelling among the tombs, and no one could bind him any longer, not even with a chain,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because he had often been bound with shackles and chains, and the chains had been torn apart by him and the shackles smashed, and no one was strong enough to subdue him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Constantly, night and day, among the tombs and in the hills, he was crying out and gashing himself with stones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he saw Jesus from a distance, he ran and bowed down before him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and crying out in a loud voice he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I put you under oath by God: do not torment me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he had been saying to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he asked him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What is your name?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “My name is Legion, for we are many.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the region.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they begged him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Send us into the pigs, so that we may enter them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he gave them permission. The unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs, and the herd, about two thousand of them, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and were drowned in the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who were herding them fled and reported it in the town and in the countryside, and people came to see what it was that had happened.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, the very man who had had the legion, and they were afraid.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man, and about the pigs.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they began to beg him to leave their territory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been demon-possessed begged him that he might be with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He did not allow him, but said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go home to your own people and report to them how much the Lord has done for you and how he has had mercy on you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a large crowd gathered around him, and he was beside the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then one of the synagogue leaders came, Jairus by name, and when he saw him he fell at his feet

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and begged him earnestly, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be saved and live.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he went with him. A large crowd was following him and pressing in on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now there was a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She had suffered much under many doctors and had spent all that she had, and she was not helped at all but instead grew worse.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having heard about Jesus, she came up behind him in the crowd and touched his cloak,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for she was saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If I touch even his clothes, I will be saved.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And immediately the source of her bleeding dried up, and she knew in her body that she was healed of the affliction.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And immediately Jesus, aware in himself that power had gone out from him, turned around in the crowd and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Who touched my clothes?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You see the crowd pressing in on you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he kept looking around to see the woman who had done this.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The woman, frightened and trembling, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell down before him and told him the whole truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Daughter, your faith has saved you. Go in peace, and be well, free of your affliction.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was still speaking, people came from the synagogue leader’s house, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Your daughter has died. Why trouble the teacher any further?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus, ignoring what was being said, told the synagogue leader,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not be afraid; only believe.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he allowed no one to accompany him except Peter and James and John, the brother of James.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to the house of the synagogue leader, and he saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went in and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child has not died but is sleeping.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they laughed at him. But he put them all out, took the child’s father and mother and those who were with him, and went in where the child was.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Taking the child by the hand, he said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Talitha koum,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which is translated,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Little girl, I say to you, get up.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And immediately the little girl stood up and began walking around, for she was twelve years old. And immediately they were beside themselves with great amazement.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He gave them strict orders that no one should know about this, and he said that she should be given something to eat.

notes.note: Manuscripts differ here between 'Gerasenes', 'Gadarenes' and 'Gergesenes'. Gerasa (modern Jerash) lay more than thirty miles from the lake, which probably led copyists to substitute places nearer the shore. 'Gerasenes' is the best-attested reading in Mark and may refer loosely to the wider region.

The verb describes the physical act of prostrating oneself before a superior, whether a god, a king or anyone whose power one acknowledges. Older versions have 'worshipped', which suggests devotion; here the gesture is one of submission from a hostile spirit. Most modern versions likewise render 'bowed down' or 'fell on his knees'.

notes.phrase: I put you under oath by God
notes.note: The verb means to bind someone by an oath, invoking a higher power to compel them. It is language exorcists themselves used against spirits (compare Acts 19:13), so there is irony in the spirit turning the formula on Jesus. Many modern versions soften it to 'I beg you' or 'swear to God'.

A legion was the largest unit of the Roman army, around five to six thousand soldiers at full strength. The word is a Latin military term borrowed into Greek. To a first-century reader it suggested an overwhelming, organised force.

'The Lord' here most naturally means God, as in the Greek Scriptures. Yet the next verse has the man proclaim what 'Jesus' had done for him, and the title could also refer to Jesus himself. Mark may intend the overlap.

The Decapolis ('Ten Cities') was a group of Hellenistic cities, mostly east of the Jordan and the Sea of Galilee, with largely Gentile populations. That setting explains the large herd of pigs, which were unclean animals under Jewish law and would not have been kept by observant Jews.

The title belonged to a lay official or patron responsible for a synagogue's building and the conduct of its meetings. It was not a governing or priestly office. 'Ruler' overstates the role for a modern reader; 'leader' is now common in recent versions.

The Greek verb means to rescue or keep safe, whether from illness, death or any other danger. Most English versions render it 'made well' or 'healed' in this chapter (verses 23, 28 and 34), which is correct for the immediate sense. 'Saved' is kept here because Mark uses different words for 'healed' and 'well' (verses 29 and 34), and because the reader would have heard the wider meaning in 'your faith has saved you'.

The phrase echoes the Greek of Leviticus 15, where a woman with a continuing discharge of blood is ritually unclean, as is anything or anyone she touches. Twelve years of this would have meant long social and religious restriction as well as illness. This helps explain why she approaches secretly and is afraid when discovered.

The word literally means a whip or scourge and was used figuratively for a tormenting illness. Older versions have 'plague', which now suggests an epidemic; 'affliction' or 'disease' is the usual modern rendering.

The verb can mean either 'overhear' or 'pay no heed to'. Most English versions choose 'overhearing', though several note the alternative. In the Greek Old Testament and in its only other New Testament occurrence (Matthew 18:17) it means to disregard or refuse to listen, and that sense suits the context, where Jesus brushes the message aside. The matter remains disputed.

These are Aramaic words, the everyday language of Jesus and of Galilee, which Mark preserves and then translates for his Greek-speaking readers. 'Talitha' is an affectionate word for a young girl; 'I say to you' is Mark's addition in the translation. The older English form 'cumi' follows manuscripts with a different form of the Aramaic imperative.
